**Paul Graham would tell you not to drop out now.** Stay in school, work on the idea as a side project, and only leave if it takes off on its own. In his view, an idea isn't enough reason to quit. Real traction is.

**His 2014 view.** In a 2014 talk to Stanford students he was blunt: "Do not start a startup in college" [1]. He gave three reasons:
- **You can't do both.** A startup takes over your whole life, so once you start one you're not really a student anymore [2].
- **Your early twenties have their own value.** It's a time for open-ended exploration: diving into projects that seem to have no payoff, or traveling cheaply with no deadline. Success takes that away. His example was Zuckerberg, whom Facebook was "running … as much as he is running Facebook" [3].
- **Waiting costs you nothing.** "You'll be more likely to succeed if you wait" [4].

**What to do with your time instead.** His advice to would-be founders in college is "just learn." Study powerful things like computer science or another hard technical field, not entrepreneurship or business. The hard part of a startup is product, and that knowledge comes from deep study [5].

**The exception.** He leaves one door open. If a side project takes off on its own, the way Facebook did, then "maybe it's reasonable to run with it" [6].

**His 2026 view.** His essay this August puts more weight on that exception. He still says a startup is incompatible with full-time study. But he points out that Microsoft and Meta both started during Harvard's reading period, and wants universities to give students more free time for side projects. If one of those projects takes off, the student has to drop it or drop out [7]. So his current position isn't "never." It's "let it prove itself first."

**Your case.** At this stage he'd tell you to build it now, while you're enrolled. Use your free time and summers, get it in front of real users, and see what happens. Dropping out on the strength of an idea is the move he warns against.

**What would change his answer:**
- **The project takes off.** If users are actually pulling it forward and it's growing faster than you can handle part-time, his own exception applies.
- **You're young enough to afford risk.** In a 2023 essay he wrote that the young can afford to try a high-variance path and find out how it goes, and that people should start taking risks early [8]. That essay doesn't mention college, though. It argues for starting young, not for quitting before the project has shown anything.

**Sources**

PG would say neither: don't start a round now just because the money is there, and don't treat "revenue" as the finish line either. What matters to him is whether the startup is visibly working. Keep building cheaply until users clearly want what you've made and your usage or growth graph is going up, then raise. Raise only enough to reach the next milestone that will convince investors.

He calls fundraising "a necessary evil" and says the people you need to impress are users, not investors [1]. In his view the best way to convince investors is to have a startup that's growing fast and simply tell them [2]. A founder who knows nothing about fundraising but has made something users love raises more easily than one who knows every trick but has a flat usage graph [3]. If you have nothing to show yet, a seed round now means pitching from weakness. Caldwell and Seibel make the same point from the other side: Seibel spent about eight months trying to raise for Justin.tv, and the team got more done in the two months after they gave up and focused on profitability [6].

He's also not asking you to bootstrap all the way to revenue as a matter of principle. He says you can still start a startup on very little money. You adjust to the money you've got, do what you can with it, and once you reach some milestone you can convince investors to give you more [4]. So the milestone is the trigger, and it doesn't have to be revenue. Users who love the product and are growing week over week count. For a hard technical startup, a credible design or a booked launch can count too. Once you do raise, he warns, don't assume the next round will be as easy [5]. That's one more reason to raise on real progress, not early hype.

Applied to you: if you can keep making product progress on what you have, do that and raise once the graph shows something. Raise now only if a specific milestone is out of reach without money, and then raise just enough to get there. Two things would change his answer. If you already have strong growth, raise now while you have leverage. If you're aiming for a modest business and not a big outcome, venture money isn't for you at all.

His essays "Ramen Profitable," "Default Alive or Default Dead" and "How to Raise Money" cover this more directly, but they aren't in the vault. From memory, not quoted: he argues that reaching ramen profitability, where revenue covers the founders' basic living costs, gives you leverage in a raise because you no longer need the money.

**Sources**

2. "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." (PG, *Lecture 3 – Before the Startup*, 2014-09-30, [9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s))

If you tell me where you are (users, growth, how many months of money you have, what the round would pay for), I can apply this to your case more specifically.

PG would tell you to go to San Francisco, at least for a while. He answered almost exactly this question in a talk in Stockholm in April 2026. Every ambitious founder asks "should I go there?", and he says the answer "is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should." You can come back later, but you should at least go [1]. He said it to a Swedish audience, but his argument doesn't depend on Sweden. To him a border is just "a dotted line on a map" [2], so Berlin is the same case.

He'd say the main reason is the people. In the Valley there are more of them, they're better, and you run into them by accident. He thinks those chance meetings are worth more than planned ones, and that things move faster because people are confident and push each other along [2][3]. He also says moving there changes you. "When you're a big fish in a small pond, you don't even know how big a fish you are." Seeing successful founders up close turns an impossible-looking goal into a hard but definite one [4][5]. There's a fundraising reason too. Investors outside the Valley assume local startups are second-rate, and he says that's true everywhere. If you leave for the Valley, it works in reverse, and you suddenly look better to investors back home [6].

He doesn't think you have to stay forever. His preferred plan is to go, ideally through YC, and then come back with a better startup, Silicon Valley money and Silicon Valley culture [7][8]. He's open about the cost: YC startups that go home are only about half as likely to become unicorns. He discounts that number himself, because the founders who stay are probably the more determined ones, and because Bay Area companies get higher valuations, not necessarily better results [9]. In the end, he says, the question that matters most is where you want your kids to grow up [10]. He also says the "Silicon Valley of Europe" job is still open, and Berlin could take it [10].

So his answer to "Berlin or SF?" is: SF now, Berlin later if you want. Building in Berlin from day one without ever going is the option he argues against. He'd only shift if you're at the stage where family and long-term home come first, and even then he'd suggest a stint in SF before settling. Keep in mind he founded YC and is recommending YC as the way to go, which he admits is "talking my own book" [8]. Sam Altman, in July 2026, agreed that moving to the Bay Area was the best way to find co-founders, but said he's less sure that still holds [11].

My own note, separate from PG: the talk doesn't cover visas, running costs or a team that's already in Berlin. Those practical issues may decide how long a stay in SF can be, even if you agree with him that you should go.

I went through the YC vault. Paul Graham never addressed a co-founder fight over a pivot directly, but his essay on persistence gives a clear answer.

**He'd tell you to persist on the goal and pivot on the means. And he'd say your co-founder's pushback is how you find out which kind of stubborn you are.** He separates two traits that look the same from the outside. Persistent people stay attached to the goal and give ground on lower-level choices when the evidence changes. Obstinate people stay attached to their first ideas about how to reach the goal [1][2]. "Keep going" is only the right answer if what you're keeping is the goal.

So split the disagreement in two. First, what is your co-founder actually asking to change?
- **The product, the approach or the channel, while keeping the same users and problem.** That's low in his "decision tree." He says the persistent "give way on any point low down in the decision tree, if its expected value drops sufficiently," and "persistence often requires that one change one's mind" [3]. If your co-founder's case rests on evidence, digging in here is obstinacy.
- **The goal itself, meaning a different problem or different users.** That's the top of the tree, where he says personal preference is legitimate and "it's ok to be irrational" [4]. If you love a problem other people don't, he thinks that often means you've noticed it matters more than they realize [4]. You can hold this ground. But then the real question is whether the two of you still share a goal, not whether to pivot.

Second, how are you reacting to their arguments? His test for obstinacy is what happens when someone points out a problem. The most determined founders he knows, the Collison brothers, "listen with an almost predatory intensity," while the obstinate tune out [5]. Before you decide, make your co-founder's strongest case better than they did. If you can't stand to, that's a warning sign.

The kind of pivot he clearly endorses is one the users drive. PayPal started as a demo for security software and became a payments company because eBay sellers wouldn't stop using it. He asks founders whether the thing on the side "could be the real product" [6]. If your co-founder is pointing at something users are pulling on, take it seriously. If the pivot is just a fresh idea because the current one is hard, his framework favors persisting. Michael Seibel puts it as: "hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely" [7].

**What would change his answer:** He'd say keep going if your current approach is the only real way to solve the problem, because then persistence and obstinacy both say don't quit [8]. He'd side with your co-founder if your evidence with users has stalled and you're defending the plan, not the goal.

**Sources**

2. "The persistent are like boats whose engines can't be throttled back. The obstinate are like boats whose rudders can't be turned." (same essay)
3. "You'll give way on any point low down in the decision tree, if its expected value drops sufficiently, but energy and resilience keep pushing you toward whatever you chose higher up." / "Indeed, persistence often requires that one change one's mind." (same essay)
4. "It's ok to be irrational near the top of the decision tree." / "When we love a problem that other people don't, it's often because we've unconsciously noticed that it's more important than they realize." (same essay)
5. "I can't think of anyone more determined than the Collison brothers, and when you point out a problem to them, they not only listen, but listen with an almost predatory intensity." (same essay)

**Launch the tiny version this week.** Paul Graham would tell you that building the full-featured product first is your intuition misleading you. Until real users have something in their hands, you don't know if you've made something people want. That is the only thing that counts. Everything else is "playing house."

**His reasoning, applied to your case.** He says startups are so counterintuitive that following your instincts leads you astray [1]. "Finish it so it's good enough to show" is one of those instincts. In his view you only prosper to the extent you make something people want [2], and you impress users "with prototypes, not words" [3]. A product you're still polishing is words. He also starts every office-hours conversation by asking for your growth rate, because it shows whether you've built the right thing [4]. With no launch, you have no growth rate and nothing to steer by.

**AI doesn't change this.** In September 2026 he said that even with powerful AI tools, many startups in the current YC batch "are not shipping fast enough" [5]. He thinks the fundamentals of startups haven't moved. Holding back for more features is exactly the mistake he's describing. His colleague Michael Seibel puts the YC line most bluntly: "launch something bad quickly." Seibel also counts getting any customer as a launch, so this week's launch doesn't need press [6]. Seibel adds that founders who wait for "the full thing" often learn the full thing isn't what customers wanted [7].

**What to actually do.** Get the smallest version that solves the core problem into the hands of the specific people who have that problem. Keep your goal fixed and treat the features as negotiable. Graham says persistent founders are attached to the goal, while obstinate ones are attached to their ideas about how to reach it [8]. A full feature list written before launch is one of those ideas.

**What would change his answer:** a product that's useless or unsafe below some threshold, like hardware or regulated finance or health. Seibel says those can't launch this fast [6]. Even then, Graham would push you to put whatever prototype you can in front of a real user now.

Paul Graham would tell you to start the startup now. He doesn't just disagree with "work at Google for a few years to learn first." He used to give that advice himself, and in 2014 he named it as one of the things he got wrong early on [1]. His reason is that you learn how to start a startup fastest by trying to start one. You may not succeed, but you'll learn faster than you would watching from inside another company [1]. He said the same thing again in August 2026: "The only way to learn how to start a startup is to do it" [2].

The rest of his thinking points the same way. He thinks the hard part of a startup is product: knowing what to build and being able to build it [2]. What you need is expertise in your own users, not expertise in startups or big companies [3]. A few years at Google will teach you how to run a large organization, and he puts that in the same bin as business school, which teaches management, "a problem that you only have in a startup if you're sufficiently successful" [3]. He also thinks luck matters more when you work on your own, so you should take several shots and start taking risks early [4]. Big efforts are best made when you're young and don't yet have children [4]. Each year at Google is a year less for those shots. And he doesn't believe you need a job doing X to learn X, since "often you can just start doing it in some form yourself" [5].

He'd also say you can't find out in advance whether you're cut out for it, at Google or anywhere else. A startup changes you, so what you're really estimating is who you could become, and the only way to find out is to try [6].

Some things would change his answer:
- **You're still a full-time student.** He says a startup and full-time study don't mix [2].
- **You're absolutely terrified of starting one.** Then he says you probably shouldn't, unless you're someone who gets off on doing things you're afraid of [6].
- **You can't afford the risk** (dependents, debt). He says most people are better off in the pool. The high-variance path suits people who know they're very good, or people, especially the young, who can afford to try and find out [4].
- **You don't have an idea that could get big.** This one comes from other YC partners, not Graham. Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel say that if you can't see how to make your idea ambitious, it may be better to work somewhere ambitious first than to spend years on something you know can't be big [7]. That's a different reason for taking the job than "learning how startups work," which is the reason Graham dropped.

**Paul Graham would tell you to work on the hard, ambitious idea, as long as it genuinely interests you and you can afford the risk.** He'd also reject the idea that the ambitious path has to mean years without results. Start it small, ship fast, and judge it by its growth rate, as you would any other startup.

He'd see "an AI tool that makes money now" as the choice he warns about. He says the best ideas are outliers you'd miss "if you were consciously looking for ways to make money" [1]. Choosing work mainly for what it pays puts you among people who chose it for the same reason [2]. He describes a "midwit peak": if you want a modest income, work on what pays. But if you want a really big outcome, or you want to do great work, and you're young and good at technology, working on what interests you most becomes the right move again [3]. He also thinks squeezing money out of customers gets you 2x at most, while making something new for them can get 10x or 100x [4]. **Paul Graham would tell you to stay small.** Raising a seed round doesn't change the rule: ideally your startup is already working before you hire even two or three people. He points to Airbnb, which took five months to hire its first employee [1].

His reasoning is that management is a problem a startup only has once it's successful [2]. Hiring early mostly gives you that problem sooner. The people you do bring on first should be "almost like founders": self-motivated peers who want the same things you do and need little managing [3][4]. Choose them the way you'd choose friends. Prefer people you've known long enough to be sure of, because the only real test of working together is having done it [5][6]. He makes one exception: someone with a narrow expertise you can't get any other way. That person may be worth hiring and supporting even if they need a lot of managing [4].

The money is runway, not a hiring mandate. In 2026 he said you "adjust for how much money you've got": spend it on reaching the next milestone, and that milestone is what gets investors to give you more [7]. He also doesn't think more people means faster shipping. Founders in the current batch have powerful AI tools and many still don't ship fast enough, because speed also depends on coming up with the ideas, not just producing the work [8]. He said this in 2026 as well as 2014: "almost everything is exactly the same" in startups [8].

He'd tell you to watch your growth rate [9]. If you're growing fast and people are clearly the bottleneck, hire, but only founder-like people and only for that bottleneck. If growth isn't there yet, more people won't fix it. A smaller team means more runway to find what users want.

PG would tell you to work on the idea you're passionate about, as long as it's a startup you're aiming to make huge and other people would actually want it. He'd also tell you to stop worrying about market size this early.

His general answer to "follow your passion?" is that it depends. The question always has a hidden "instead of," and if your goal is ordinary money, you usually can't afford to work on what interests you most, because people pay you for what they want, not what you want [1]. But he calls this a "midwit peak." If you want to get really rich, and you're young and good at technology, working on what interests you most becomes the right move again [2]. That's not because passion keeps you motivated. It's because the big money comes from startups, and the best startup ideas are outliers you'd skip if you were consciously hunting for ways to make money. Apple, Google and Facebook all started as projects their founders did for fun [3]. He doesn't think diligence can substitute: to do something exceptionally well, you have to be interested in it [4].

He's equally clear about the "bigger market" side. Don't worry about the second number, market size. If you're building something you and people like you want, you're predicting future demand, so the market grows into you. You can always expand into nearby markets once you have a beachhead [5]. To him, a big market on paper is a weak reason to pick an idea, and the "bad but plausible-sounding" ideas you get by looking for them consciously tend to come with big-market slides [6]. He also warns that if you pick work mainly for the payoff, you'll be surrounded by people who picked it for the same reason [7].

Two conditions apply. First, being passionate isn't enough. He'd want to know whether a real group of users wants the thing too, because users are the only test that counts [8]. Second, if you honestly can't tell which idea is better, he'd say that's ignorance, not a real tie. The fix is to start working on both in some small form and see which one pulls you in and gets real users [9].

What would change his answer: if your goal is a solid income rather than a big outcome, he'd say you usually can't afford to follow your interest. And if you've built the passion idea and nobody besides you wants it, the user test overrides everything else.

Apply to YC. Paul Graham never answers "YC or angels?" head-on, but everything he says points the same way. He also wouldn't see it as one or the other: YC began as an angel firm [4], and getting in is what makes other investors line up. Of investors outside the Valley he says that "as soon as you tell them that you've been accepted by Y Combinator, often they're suddenly... they're tripping over themselves to try and invest in you" [1]. So in his view YC isn't the alternative to an angel round. It's the easiest way to get one on good terms.

His deeper point is that fundraising skill hardly matters. He calls fundraising "merely a necessary evil" and says the people to impress are users, not investors [5]. The way to convince investors is to be growing fast "and then simply tell investors so" [2]. He doesn't think founders need to learn how an angel round works, since Zuckerberg probably didn't either [3]. Raising straight from angels means pitching, chasing and negotiating, which is the part of startups he thinks matters least. Michael Seibel describes spending about eight months failing to raise for Justin.tv, and says the team got more done in the last two months, once it stopped pitching, than in all the months before [9]. YC also gives you what a check alone doesn't: colleagues where a startup is usually "a very lonely business", batchmates who have already solved your technical problem, and a ready market of "early adopters who decide quickly" [6]. He calls YC the best way to go to Silicon Valley for a while and then come back [7]. He also thinks the Valley changes you, not just your fundraising [8].

What would change his answer: if you're already growing fast and investors are chasing you, his rule that you raise by doing well and saying so works without YC, and raising straight from angels is fine [2]. Either way, applying costs very little. Don't spend months on a deck. Apply, and keep building while you wait to hear back.

One caution, which he raises himself: he founded YC, and when he tells founders to come he says "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book" [7].

Paul Graham would tell you to have co-founders, but not to treat "find a co-founder" as a step you finish before you begin. Start building now, with people you already like and respect. Working on the project together is how you find your co-founder. Don't recruit a stranger just so you have one, and don't plan on staying solo.

His view is that "the most successful startups tend to have multiple founders" [1]. He also says you can't tell from a meeting whether someone will be a good co-founder: "the only way to tell for sure if someone will be good to work with is to work with them". Apple and Microsoft were just the last of many projects their founders had built together [1]. That's why he rejects "wait for a co-founder" as a separate phase. He tells people to work on problems that interest them, with people they like and respect, and says that's how you end up with "co-founders at the same time as the idea" [2]. When you choose, pick the way you'd pick friends. Choose people you've known long enough to be sure of, because "a lot of people … are really good at seeming likeable for a while" [3].

Other YC partners give the same verdict for a different reason. Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel (2026) say founders mostly die by losing hope and giving up. A solo founder has nobody to talk to and no shared sense of mission [4]. The single founders they've seen succeed all built "co-founder-like" relationships with employees, advisors or friends to fill that gap [5]. So if you do start alone, plan on building that support yourself.

Here's what would change the answer. If you've worked on projects with nobody you'd trust, PG would say start the project alone rather than pair up with a stranger, and bring people in as you work with them. Garry Tan (August 2026) pushes this further. He argues that a founder using AI agents is "already running an organization" before having a co-founder [6]. That makes starting solo more workable, but even Tan doesn't say you should skip co-founders altogether.
